chunks: Fiducials on a PCB. The question: What are fiducials?
Fiducials are small marks on a circuit board, usually a dot of bare copper about 1 mm across, that a machine's camera can find.
Assembly machines use them to learn exactly where the board really sits.
Without them, a machine would assume the board is perfectly positioned and perfectly square, and it never is.
Think of the corner marks printed on a page that a scanner uses to straighten the image. The scanner does not trust that you laid the paper down perfectly.
It looks for the marks and corrects for any shift or tilt.
A placement machine does the same with fiducials: it finds the dots, works out how the board is shifted, turned or slightly stretched, and adjusts where it puts every part.
Unlike paper, a board is rigid, so the stretch is tiny but still matters.
Left, a board with three asymmetric global fiducials (filled dots at three corners, none in the fourth) and a pair of local fiducials (orange) diagonally across a fine-pitch QFP.
Right, the fiducial itself: a solid copper disc in a larger solder-mask opening. The empty space around the copper is what gives the camera its contrast.
Fiducial: an alignment mark that a camera locates. Global fiducial: a mark in the corners of the board or panel that fixes its overall position, rotation and size.
Local fiducial: a mark beside one fine-pitch part to correct that spot more precisely.
Solder-mask opening: a cleared area in the colored coating, so the copper dot shows up with strong contrast.
Pick-and-place: the machine that picks up parts and sets them on the board.
Suppose the board sits on the conveyor turned by 0. 1 degree. A part 100 mm from the pivot is then off by about 0. 17 mm. A chip with 0.
5 mm pin spacing has pads (the copper spots its pins are soldered to) only about 0. 25 mm wide, so that error could bridge two pins.
The camera measures two or three fiducials, the machine computes the shift, tilt and stretch, and it corrects every placement. That is the whole idea.
"Fiducials are alignment marks on a board, typically a 1 mm bare-copper dot with a clear mask opening around it, that a camera uses to find the real position of the board.
The paste printer, pick-and-place and AOI use them to correct for offset, rotation and scale.
Global fiducials on the panel or board corners fix the whole board, and local ones near fine-pitch parts refine placement of that part.
They need clean contrast, so no silkscreen or traces nearby, and the global ones should be asymmetric so the board can't be loaded backwards."
